utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to ask for a private session, because the witness who is going to testify this afternoon has asked for protective measures, and a request to that effect has been submitted to you on the 23rd of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any objection? The application is for a pseudonym and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no objection, Your Honours, if it's a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll make the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, we started late because the Trial Chamber had another matter to deal with which I'm afraid did not finish today and will have to go over until tomorrow, so we shall be rather late starting tomorrow. We can sit until just before half past 4.00, when colleagues have another meeting. So if you could tailor your evidence around those times, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we've discussed this, and we can sit until 4.45. We can see if we can get through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Sorry to keep you. If you would like to take the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat. Very well. The pseudonym is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pseudonym for this witness will be Witness Q.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The legal officer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we for a moment remain in private session when referring to questions which provide information on the identification of the witness? That will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Q, while performing your duties in the police station of Novi Travnik, when you returned there, your superior was of Croat ethnicity, and his name was Zlatan Civcija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992, you saw Mr. Zlatan Civcija wearing a camouflage uniform and HVO insignia and coming to the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, quite so, though this was not customary. I think that he was the first among the policemen to start going to work, that is, coming to the police station in a camouflage uniform while everyone else wore blue uniforms of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 19th of June, 1992, the police station where you were working, together with your Croatian colleagues, was attacked, as well as the headquarters of the Territorial Defence in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, because the TO headquarters and the police station premises were actually in one and the same building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following this attack by HVO forces, you and your colleagues of Muslim ethnicity left the station, where you were no longer allowed to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. We relocated to other premises, actually to the premises of the kindergarten, so we moved out of the so-called lower part of the city which, after all this, was under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As of this first conflict which happened in June 1992, you saw, coming to the police station, Muslims from Novi Travnik who came regularly to complain either because they were robbed or exposed to violence by members of the HVO and the HOS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. People would come who had any kind of problems. The most frequent complaints were incursions by men in uniform, belonging to the HVO and the HOS, into their apartments. All they could do was complain, and these complaints of theirs were registered in the form of official reports in our police station at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This collection of complaints continued throughout the second half of 1992 and throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you now some documents, Witness Q, to ask you to look at them and to comment on them. The documents have reference number Z1963,1 and Z1963,12. Do you have the document 1963,1 before you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is, indeed, a record written by you, is it not, on the 10th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, it is a -- if I may add, it is an official note compiled in connection with the expulsion of Muslims from the lower part of the town, that is, the part that was under the control of the HVO at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there's no point in showing the document on the ELMO because it bears the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you to look through the other documents, Exhibit number 1963,12. There are about 40 notes on offences drawn up by the Novi Travnik police station.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you been able to look through these documents quickly? Do you recognise those documents as being issued by the police station that you belonged to at the time, the one that had to move after 19 June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise the documents. They are mostly official notes compiled by officials of the police, police officers, on the basis of complaints by citizens, mostly having to do with their expulsion and their harassment by members of the HVO. That was a way for us to document each of these events, of course, those that were reported to us, though I believe there were many more that were never reported to anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of these reports bear the signature of the investigator, such as, for example, a report signed by Mr. Enver Hodzic or by Mr. Semin Kalbic. Were they colleagues from your police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, these were colleagues. Enver Hodzic worked in the criminal police of the Public Security Station in Novi Travnik, and Semin Kalbic also worked as a criminal technician at the time, though he also performed other police duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Several of these reports do not bear any name of the person who drafted them but simply a wording -- simply the words "Authorised Official" is indicated. Could you explain this to us, what it means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. This was frequent because the relocated police station was virtually on the very front line, so many policemen, for this reason, did not sign these reports because one didn't know under whose control that same station might be the very next day, the police station. The other reason is that this kind of keeping records of a criminal offence or an act has the same validity with the judicial bodies. What is important is the act itself and not the signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In most of these reports, the perpetrators, whether they are robberies, forced expulsions, or harassment, are often described as being masked. Could you explain that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. In these official notes, it is stated, as was in fact the case, that perpetrators used to coexist with their neighbours, Bosniaks, so they could be readily recognised by the victims, to call them that. On the other hand, the effect was greater on those victims, forcing them to leave their apartments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In one of these reports, appearing in the pile of documents submitted to you, dated the 28th of January, 1993, reference is made to a robbery carried out in the premises of Mr. Ragib Zukic. It is a document on page 27 in the English version and 27 in the Bosniak version as well, Z1963.12, page 27.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is stated in this report that Mr. Ragib Zukic had to swallow and drink detergent. Was that a normal practice? You didn't hear my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No, I didn't get the translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it. In this note that you have in front of you, it is stated that the victim, Mr. Ragib Zukic, had to swallow detergent, that he was forced to do so on the part of persons who appeared there. Was this something normal? Did you have other complaints of this kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I personally do not recall any other cases of such abuse. All I can say is that these notes are authentic, and I know Ragib Zukic personally. He was once beaten up also as a member of a negotiating team; I think it was on the 19th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This gentleman, Mr. Ragib Zukic, that you are mentioning, he was a member of a Muslim commission that was negotiating with the HVO on the 19th of October, 1992, at the Worker's Centre in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, he was one of the members, and more or less, all the citizens of Novi Travnik know that with the president of the party, I think it was Salih Krnjic, that he was beaten up in the Worker's Centre in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you, before we finish with these documents, to look at the last pages of the pile that has been given to you, pages 37 to 40 of this document. It appears, reading these notes on offences, that on four of these, there are certain anomalies regarding the dates. The document is dated the 25th of January, and it says that the victim appeared on the 26th, for instance. On page 38, the document dated the 23rd of January says that the facts, that is, the fire of the victim's house, occurred on the 20th of October, 1993, which means much later. Again, page 39, the report is dated the 25th of November, 1992, and it says that the event occurred on the 20th of January, 1992. Can you give us some explanations regarding these discrepancies with respect to the dates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I think that this happened mostly due to errors made by the policeman writing the official reports. We have to bear in mind the period when these reports were written, the position of the police station itself on the very front line which was a daily target of the HVO. So it is quite possible that such mistakes can be made here and there, but I'm quite sure that the contents of all these notes correspond to the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you well, the discrepancies that we have referred to are purely of a formal nature due to the lack of concentration, which is understandable, on the part of the person drafting them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have finished with these documents, Mr. Witness, so, Mr. Usher, you can collect them. We've finished with this document, but there will be others to be shown to the witness. In the period we're talking about, that is, the end of 1992 and the first six months of 1993, did you have occasion to see on television the accused Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I did, yes, on several occasions. I was able to see him on television and hear various statements that he made, which sounded rather like propaganda to the effect that parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina inhabited by Croats were Croatia, they were Croatia and will remain Croatia, or words to that effect, and that is how I remember his public statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you recall, for the benefit of Their Honours, the words spoken by the accused, as you have just said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I can -- it is difficult for me to recall any further detail apart from what I have already said. I remember that he often wore a camouflage uniform with HVO patches. I never met him personally, however.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say on television that the Croatian Community --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let the witness give the evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he speak about the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna during these speeches on television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He spoke about the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what he said with reference to that Croatian Community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you did not know Mr. Dario Kordic personally. Did you know the accused Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No. I do not know them, because as I have already said, I came to Bosnia just before the outbreak of the war, so that I don't know many of the inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: (redacted) with a reference number Z1963,7. Do you see that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You appear on the right-hand side of this document, at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No, I was never a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This must be a mistake in the drafting. I think this was a uniform form of the HVO of Novi Travnik, of the commission for exchange, because at the bottom, where it says that the dead bodies of civilians were received, I think it would be more correct to say "-" rather than -- it should be "/" rather than "-" after it says, "HVO Members - Civilians."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this title of being a member of the BH army was given to you by mistake by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: They could have put down whatever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to talk about this exchange of prisoners and bodies. These exchanges most frequently took place in dangerous places and very close to the front line, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, that was most frequently the case. It was on the line of separation mostly and close to a place called Trenica, which is close to the town of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Lazine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to show you a document with reference number 1963,3.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is specified in this document that the soldiers whose bodies were exchanged were mutilated and tortured. Can you give us some more details regarding the condition of these bodies of those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: As far as these soldiers are concerned, I know that they were captured on the 29th of June when the HVO attacked the village of Lazine. As usual, we negotiated the exchange for these bodies. At first, we had information that they had been captured alive, and this surprised us a little, and we were surprised when we were given them as dead during the exchange. The exchange was carried out close to the locality of Trenica in the Novi Travnik municipality. As on previous occasions when there were exchanges, the immediate family would usually identify the bodies being exchanged, and a doctor found on the spot. In this case, it was Dr. Suvad Grizic, who was also the coroner. I personally did not look at the bodies being exchanged because it was far from a pleasant sight, because the stench was terrible, and also the reactions of family members was terribly moving. If UNPROFOR vehicles were used for transportation, I had to go back to town quickly. In this case, the coroner, Grizic, gave me a detailed description of the condition of the exchanged bodies, Muhamed Sahinovic, Hajdar Mujic, Enver Omeragic, and Besim Omeragic, as is stated in this report. I remember that according to what Muhamed Sahinovic's brother told me, that is, Bakir Sahinovic, the bodies were in some kind of nylon and they were wet, and he had the impression that they had been washed, the bodies had been washed, before being exchanged. Later on, when Bakir transported his brother Muhamed from the nylon to the grave, he noticed that his underwear was red, soaked with blood, and that a part was missing near the sex organ. In fact, half of it had been cut off. That is what made me remember this particular exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should now like to show you another document, that is, document 1963,11.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get information from a Mr. Ibrisimbegovic about a detention camp that was in the Stojkovici region; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. This is my own official note, and it was compiled after the talk with Safet Ibrisimbegovic who was at the time imprisoned in the camp at Stojkovici. This is one of the ways, as I have already said, of how we documented certain reports pertaining to the events that had taken place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the information which you received from that Mr. Ibrisimbegovic, the soldiers whose bodies were given back on the 8th of July, 1993, could they have been kept in that camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: In view of the fact that he spent from the 13th to the 19th of July in the camp, then there is great probability that this could have happened because they were taken prisoner on the 29th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I didn't quite understand. This Mr. Ibrisimbegovic was detained, according to the report, on the 5th of July at least and on the 18th of July. On the 5th of July, he was in that camp; do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: It says that he was there from the 13th of June up until the 19th of July, and this is what he stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that there is a slight mistake in the English interpretation. It says that he was detained from the 13th to the 19th of July in the camp, whereas, in fact, it was the 13th of June to the 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: This is the original official note, and I think that it states in precise terms the time in which he -- the time he spent there, and I should like to say that this was his statement taken as an official note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we can read the note. We don't need to go through it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like us now to speak about another fact which occurred a little bit later, that is, the events that took place in October of 1993. Do you remember that at that time, three soldiers of the Novi Travnik Brigade, of the 308th BH Army Brigade, were forced to walk toward their own front line by HVO soldiers, whereas they had been attached to mines.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that event. It took place on the 3rd -- I think it was the 3rd of October, yes -- that five of them were taken prisoner by the HVO during the HVO attack on the village of Isakovici in Novi Travnik, and two days after that, that is to say, on the 5th of October, three of them were forced to carry mines, explosive devices, mortars on their backs and to move towards the positions of the BH army. I remember that when they reached the vicinity of this position, the mines, the explosive devices were activated, and they were on their backs. Then the soldiers of the army succeeded in getting the remains of Enes Hajric, whereas the remains of Muslimovic and Mujak, the other two men, they were not able to gather up the remains, so that their bodily remains stayed on no man's land for about 40 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself participate in the operations which allowed the remains of the two soldiers to be collected?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you escorted by a British officer whose name was Yorke?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. On the occasion, I was greatly helped by Captain Yorke who did his utmost to help pull out the bodily remains of those individuals with the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, the HVO, so that we did succeed on that day in doing so; I think it was the 15th of November. We succeeded in recuperating the bodily remains of these people. Great efforts were invested to do so. It was already growing dark, it had already grown dark, and the captain did not move about in his vehicle at dark, but nonetheless --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It isn't necessary to give us those details, Witness Q. Thank you. I'm going to give you a document which was drafted by an officer of the British Battalion whose name was Yorke, that is, document 1963,10. This is a document in English. I'm going to read out a passage from the document, and it says that Captain Yorke spoke to an individual who was responsible for exchanges, the name given is your own, and then on the second page, it says what observations were made by that officer, particularly the fact that near the remains of the bodies cables were found which led directly to the HVO lines. As far as you know, does this report match the facts that we're speaking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: As far as my personal participation in all this is concerned, I said that I was not personally on the spot when the bodies -- that is to say, at Begino Brdo when the bodies were dismembered. Captain Yorke and a journalist of the BH army, Enes Begic was his name -- I came to a place called Isakovici, I got there in Captain Yorke's Land Rover, and that's where I waited for them -- and the two of them went to collect the remains which they then brought back to the building, the secondary school building in the upper part of town, and that is when Enes Begic made a videotape of the bodily remains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the report, it says that you were a military policeman. What would you have to say about that characterisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No. No, that's not true. I think that there has been an error. As I said previously, I was never a member of the BH army. I was always a member of the Public Security Station, that is to say, the civilian police station. Perhaps Captain Yorke made a mistake because of the clothing that I wore most frequently which was a camouflage uniform, because at the time, it was the most apt thing to wear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to speak about other matters now which have to do with the building that was known as Stari Soliter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, let me interrupt you to say this, if it assists: We have evidence about the attack on Stari Soliter, which was, as I recollect, uncontradicted. So you can take it fairly quickly until we get to the witness's own part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, Mr. President, only one witness mentioned this, that was on the 16th of April of this year, that is, Witness C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean. We don't need to hear it all again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, in order to expedite matters, I would like to show several other documents which the witness drafted and which have to do with what happened in Stari Soliter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you yourself involved in the relations with the residents of that building in Novi Travnik between the 9th of June, 1993 and the 17th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I was directly involved in the negotiations concerning the release of those individuals from the building, and I took certain steps, made certain efforts in that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards the living conditions of those people during the three months when they were in that building, they were very difficult; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, they were very difficult. For all practical purposes, the building was exposed to daily fire of the members of the HVO. Apart from that, it was impossible to get food because there was only one entrance to the building, and so from that side, they were in fact -- they were in fact prisoners, just for having been in their own apartments when it started. It was the children that suffered in particular. The youngest child was only 11 months old, a baby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the beginning, there were 57 people in that building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning, there were 57 people, right up until the 1st of July. On the 1st of July, when the attack was launched by the members of the HVO and the HV, their attack on the building, Zijad Muslic, a resident, was wounded and so was a member of the Croatian army, Marko Suhreta, so that we had to evacuate them. We were allowed, probably by the HVO, to evacuate these people because Marko Suhreta was wounded, so that there were only 56 residents in the building after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a quick look at the document that I'm going to show you? First, 1963,4 and 1963,5.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, it is -- they are reports in fact which I submitted to the war presidency of the municipality of Novi Travnik relating to the problems of the Stari Soliter building, and they were in fact my efforts to find a solution to the problem, to stop the suffering of the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm now going to show you 1963,6, which is dated 1 August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the author of this document as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It deals with the delivery of food after a long period of deprivation for the residents of the building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This is a report which states that after a series of negotiations with the Croatian side, "... we succeeded on the 1st of August, through UNPROFOR mediation, to bring food to the Stari Soliter building ..." because the situation was getting worse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to show you a document which is dated 3 July, with the reference number 1963,2. You already mentioned some of these facts, but particularly the presence of a soldier of the Croatian army -- I'm saying "the Croatian army," that is, from the Republic of Croatia -- who was wounded in the Stari Soliter building at the beginning of July 1993 in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The soldier was a soldier of the Croatian army, because at the time we found an ID on him which stated that he was a member of that particular army. So he was not a member of the HVO but of the HV, as we called it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. That was a request made by the Croatian side, to allow the civilians from the building to be freed on the condition that all the Croats living in the villages mentioned should cross over to the lower part of town, that is to say, the part of town that was under HVO control. However, the Bosnian side did not agree to that at the beginning, because in actual fact this would have meant ethnic cleansing of the area, that on the one hand, and on the other, a certain number of Croats did not wish to be exchanged, and it was very difficult for us to convince the HVO commission that these people did not wish to be exchanged, quite simply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you yourself in a position where you were to meet those people and to hear what they had to say? I would now like to show you documents which refer to what we're speaking about. These are documents 1963,8 and 1963,9.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. 1963,8, this is a statement by which the signatory claims that he does not wish to be exchanged, and he says that -- and I did this at the request of the HVO commission, because they didn't believe me that a certain number of individuals quite simply did not wish to be exchanged, especially the elderly population. This can also be seen in the second document. It is a list of individuals who stated that they did not wish to be exchanged, the offer or principle, and I personally contacted many of them. I remember it well. I remember Mate Ljubas from the village of Torine who did not wish to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the end, after the 17th of September, the exchange took place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those exchanges and discussions with representatives of the HVO, did they lead you to understanding that they had received instructions in order to carry out the exchange?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes. For their part, Josip Udovicic was the representative, and the exchange took place in town up at the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Q, let me introduce myself. My name is Mitko Naumovski, a lawyer from Zagreb, and I am one of the Defence counsel for Mr. Dario Kordic. In view of the fact that we sometimes have problems with the interpretations, you and I can understand each other as soon as we say something, but please wait for the interpretation before you answer my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness Q, as far as I was able to gather, you have given a statement to the investigators of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you give a statement and discuss this question with the state committee for the investigation of war crimes attached to the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you make a statement to the so-called Agency for Investigation Documentation, AID?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Q, as a policeman, you trained in the Republic of Croatia, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, among other things in Croatia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you worked as a member of the Ministry of Defence in Sibenik until 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No, that's a mistake. No, that's not true. I was never a member of the Defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I mean the Internal Affairs ministry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, the Internal Affairs ministry, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps I misspoke. I meant the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In 1991, you therefore came to work as a policeman in Novi Travnik, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Your family stayed on to live in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No, they came with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did they live with you throughout in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about the first conflict that occurred on the 19th of June, 1992. Their Honours have already had occasion to hear about it. Just one more question about it. Do you know that prior to the 19th of June was an incident that occurred on the 18th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So you know nothing about the incident that occurred on the 18th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No. I know that the overall situation was very tense. I am unable, however, to pinpoint a particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But if you don't know the details, I won't go into that. But let us clarify for the record, in the same building was both the Novi Travnik police station and the command of the Territorial Defence, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. It was one and the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, at the time of the second conflict, you were not in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I was within the territory of Novi Travnik municipality but not in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You were in the village of Zagrlje, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But at the beginning of October 1992, you were not in the territory of Novi Travnik municipality at all, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Immediately before the conflict, I was in Croatia with my family. I came on the 18th of October from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Let us be very precise. You went to the Republic of Croatia with your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm asking you because in your statement for the investigators, you stated that you were visiting family members in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, my wife's family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So the wife's family live in Croatia and not your wife and children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: My wife's family is living in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In that case, I will not ask you much about the second statement, as you were not in the town itself. But as you were in Zagrlje, if I understand correctly, which is relatively close to Opara, about some 15 kilometres away, my question is would you agree with me that the Muslims in this village -- in Zagrlje and Opara expelled the Serbs on the 27th of August, 1993, just before you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I don't know which village you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Serbs who lived there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I said that I came from Croatia in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you about August 1992. At that time, you were working as a policeman in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Do you know or would you agree with me that on the 27th of August, 1992, the Muslims expelled the Serbs from Zagrlje and Opara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I do not agree with that statement. I don't know that the Serbs were expelled. Those who had lived there abandoned those places before the conflict, abandoned the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Before which conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Before the conflict between the army and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Which conflict are you referring to, June 1992, the first incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the second incident, October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mentioning these conflicts, could you tell us with precision when the front line was established in the town of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: The front line was established after -- I think it was after the second conflict, after October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Tell us, please, in a few words, about your work as a policeman. Until the 19th of June, 1992, you worked in one police station, and after that date, the police separated, if we can call it that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: We were expelled from that police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But I would put it differently. You left that station yourselves because you didn't want to work there; nobody forced you out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: In my view, that is a leading question and, I think, unacceptable. We left the station after we had been attacked with arms, with rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: We were speaking about the building and the conflict linked to that building, but you personally were not thrown out of the police station. That is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I wonder if we're going to get much further with this. You've heard the witness's evidence, you've challenged it, and you can call other evidence, if you have any. I don't think we'll be assisted by any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what exactly you did as a policeman in the newly-formed police station in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. But were you a patrolling policeman or were you engaged in administrative affairs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I engaged in police affairs. You know very well; it was a war. You do what the police does. There was a shortage of manpower.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Tell me, please, can we agree on a further point, and that is that in September 1992, because of the war operations going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole, between four and five thousand Muslim refugees came to the town and the municipality of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Which refugees, from where?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The refugees from the areas where the Serbs were expelling populations, the north and northwest of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, there were refugees coming especially from the municipality of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes. That wave of refugees from Jajce came when Jajce fell, but I'm talking about the second half of 1992, refugees were arriving. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know when they left. I can't be precise about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But as a policeman, dealing with people on a daily basis, you must have noticed that in September 1992, there was a great deal of pressure from the refugees in the town and the surroundings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: There were refugees, but I cannot be specific about when they came or when they left. I know that most of them came when the Serbs attacked the municipality of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Tell me, please, these refugees that came to the territory of Novi Travnik, did they report to the Novi Travnik police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: There were records.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Apart from being registered, they all submitted requests for ID cards because they had moved into certain apartments in town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You weren't engaged on those matters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, the Prosecutor has tendered into evidence a large number of official notes with statements by citizens complaining about what had happened to them, robberies, and so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Are you asking me as the police or me personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, the police. You said you and your colleagues, because we know that there were many documents that were not written by you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the ways. You know that, according to our legislation, an official note is a manner of registering an event, and so I received such notes and complaints.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: A brief overview of these documents -- there are many; I haven't had time to look into them -- but I see that they are official notes, and that was all that was taken, a mere matter of registering the event.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, because what else could we do in those days? Could I perhaps call up someone to assist us? That was all that we could do because we had no one to complain to on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: The citizens did not write those statements they gave, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: These were statements in the form of official notes, so they are not really statements. They are, rather, official notes about statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. But members of which ethnic group complained to your police station about what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Mostly Bosnian Muslims, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: To judge by the names, the vast majority are Muslims; I just wanted us to agree on that. Tell me, please, regarding your particular field of activity, did the Kalinska Ulica belong to your area? It was previously called the 4th of July Street.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: These are buildings, apartment buildings inhabited by other ethnic groups, I mean, Croats and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Those citizens in those apartment buildings were also mistreated and evicted, were they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I don't agree with you. If any one of them left, they left on time because they knew when the HVO would attack, at least in the case of the first and second conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: When you say "on time," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I mean they simply knew that a conflict would occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness Q, I'm not talking about the conflict. I'm asking you whether you know or, rather, whether you would agree with me that both Croats and Serbs living in this same street were also mistreated, people broke into their flats, their property was stolen, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No, I do not agree with you on that issue. I'm not aware of cases of Croats on Kalinska Street being mistreated or evicted. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But can we agree that as a policeman responsible for that sector, you should have been aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Listen, the witness has said he is not aware of it. We can't take the matter any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Your Honour permits, I wanted to mention two particular cases, but if you disagree, I won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no point. He says he doesn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: A few questions in connection with the events that happened in the old skyscraper or Soliter. Their Honours have already heard about it, so I shall be very brief. In your earlier statements, and you gave two, you said that the HVO attacked and shot at the building but that on one occasion, an HVO soldier, Marko Suhreta, entered the building and was wounded, together with another person; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Also today, you said, if I heard correctly, that this Marko Suhreta had documents on him that he was a Croatian soldier.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, he had the ID of a Croatian soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Did you have that ID in your hands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I saw it. I personally saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And where was it left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I don't know who has it; probably one of the tenants kept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But this Marko Suhreta, does he come from the territory of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I don't know where he comes from. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But it was for the first time that you said today that the HV attacked this apartment building. I never found that statement in your earlier statements.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I said that a member of the Croatian army participated in the attack on the Stari Soliter. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So this is this individual that we are talking about, so that there should be no misunderstanding, and I think that is a mistake in the transcript. You agreed with the question of the Prosecutor today that the HVO set a condition on the release of the occupants of that skyscraper; that is, that all the Croats on the territory under the control of the BH army should be released.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Correct. That was a precondition set by the Croatian side. It was very clear and very precise, "all for all," as they would put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness Q, I have to remind you that in your statement of the 5th of June, 1999, that is, your second statement to the investigators, you said that the HVO asked that the Croats living in their houses in Senkovici and Torine should be released to territory under Croatian control. You were talking about only the villages of Senkovici and Torine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Those were the remaining population living in the territory under the control of the BH army. You should know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I just wanted us to agree that in that statement, you did not mention any other village but the villages of Senkovici and Torine. Senkovici, yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Most of the Croatian population at the time were in the village of Senkovici. I think there were about 200 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I have seen several exhibits tendered by the Prosecutor today having to do with Croats living in the area under the control of the BH army. By way of an example, this is Z1963,8, it is a statement from which -- it is a printed form of your commission for the exchange of prisoners, from which it emerges that Petar Kuhta and Milka Kuhta refused to take part in the exchange on the 17th of September, 1993. It is number Z1963,8. Do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But there's only one signature on this statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: One of the two of them; we don't know which one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Petar Kuhta signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Then there is a heading "Witnesses," people who witnessed this statement. We agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: But no one is registered under that heading, "Witnesses"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: As you can see by the date, this was written just before the exchange. So there were objective problems prior to the exchange. There were people who simply would not be exchanged. The Croatian side wants them to be exchanged. So there were hundreds of people waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, it's now coming on to the time when we must adjourn. Have you many more questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have a few, at least another 15 or 20 minutes. I tried to be as expeditious as possible; unfortunately, I haven't succeeded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Tomorrow afternoon then. Witness Q, I'm afraid we're not going to finish your evidence today, so I must ask you to come back tomorrow to conclude it. Could you be back, please, at half past two tomorrow? Could I remind you, during that time, not to speak to anybody about your evidence and not let anybody, of course, speak to you about it? That does include members of the Prosecution. Would you be back at half past two? Is there something you want to raise, Mr. Lopez-Terres?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply wish to indicate that most of the documents that we referred to this afternoon bear the name of the witness and, therefore, they also should be protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Half past two then tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.43 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 29th of September, 1999, at 2.30 p.m. 25
